claims.claim: In mammals, the amygdala is the primary site for valence assignment during Pavlovian learning.
claims.source: In mammals, the amygdala is the primary site for valence assignment during Pavlovian learning (O'Neill et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: As a neutral sensory stimulus (conditioned stimulus [CS]) is paired with punishment or reward (unconditioned stimulus [US]), the CS acquires the capacity to evoke valence-specific response patterns in the amygdala.
claims.source: As a neutral sensory stimulus (conditioned stimulus [CS]) is paired with punishment or reward (unconditioned stimulus [US]), the CS acquires the capacity to evoke valence-specific response patterns in the amygdala (Grewe et al., 2017; Zhang and Li, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Amygdala-dependent valence-specific behaviors are mediated by distinct networks whose outputs diverge to different projection areas responsible for aversive or appetitive unconditioned responses.
claims.source: Nevertheless, it has been shown that amygdala-dependent valence-specific behaviors are mediated by distinct networks Gore et al., 2015 whose outputs diverge to different projection areas responsible for aversive or appetitive unconditioned responses (Beyeler et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: GABAergic and glutamatergic projection neurons from the lateral hypothalamus to the ventral tegmental areas (VTA) can evoke appetitive and aversive behaviors, respectively.
claims.source: For example, GABAergic and glutamatergic projection neurons from the lateral hypothalamus to the ventral tegmental areas (VTA) can evoke appetitive and aversive behaviors, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an example of convergent circuit mechanisms.

claims.claim: GABAergic and glutamatergic projection neurons from the lateral hypothalamus converge on the same population of GABAergic neurons in VTA to differentially control downstream dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
claims.source: These projection neurons converge on the same population of GABAergic neurons in VTA to differentially control downstream dopaminergic neurons (DANs) (Nieh et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: Both divergent and convergent circuit motifs are considered important for the valence-to-behavior transformation in vertebrates.
claims.source: Thus, both divergent and convergent circuit motifs are considered important for the valence-to-behavior transformation in vertebrates (Tye, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: In fly olfactory learning, the primary site for CS-US association is the mushroom body (MB).
claims.source: In fly olfactory learning, the primary site for CS-US association is the mushroom body (MB), where parallel axon fibers of the odor-encoding Kenyon cells (KCs) are segmented into a series of MB compartments that are defined by the dendrites of MB output neurons (MBONs) and axons of US-encoding DANs (Aso et al., 2014a; Tanaka et al., 2008; Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Population activity of KCs represents odor identity.
claims.source: While population activity of KCs represents odor identity (Campbell et al., 2013), that of MBONs is less effective in doing so (Hige et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: Population activity of MBONs is less effective in representing odor identity than KCs.
claims.source: While population activity of KCs represents odor identity (Campbell et al., 2013), that of MBONs is less effective in doing so (Hige et al., 2015b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: Individual MBONs encode the valence of stimuli.
claims.source: Instead, individual MBONs are considered to encode the valence of stimuli because optogenetic activation of each type of MBONs can elicit either approach or avoidance behavior (Aso et al., 2014b; Owald et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: MBONs do not appear to command specific motor sequences because their activation does not induce stereotyped motor patterns.
claims.source: However, MBONs do not appear to command specific motor sequences because their activation does not induce stereotyped motor patterns (Aso et al., 2014b).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: When flies were repeatedly trained by pairing one of two odors with optogenetic activation of sugar sensory neurons, flies gradually increased upwind locomotion in response to the paired odor.
claims.source: When flies were repeatedly trained by pairing one of two odors with optogenetic activation of sugar sensory neurons, flies gradually increased upwind locomotion in response to the paired odor but developed odor preference in the binary choice more rapidly (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claims.claim: Flies developed odor preference in binary choice more rapidly than upwind locomotion when trained by pairing odor with optogenetic activation of sugar sensory neurons.
claims.source: When flies were repeatedly trained by pairing one of two odors with optogenetic activation of sugar sensory neurons, flies gradually increased upwind locomotion in response to the paired odor but developed odor preference in the binary choice more rapidly (Figure 1D–E).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1D-E.

claims.claim: The learning rate measured by odor preference was much faster than that measured by upwind locomotion.
claims.source: As a result, the learning rate measured by odor preference was much faster than that measured by upwind locomotion (Figure 1F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claims.claim: Memories in the γ5β′2a and the γ4 failed to promote significant upwind movement.
claims.source: Despite robust CS+ preference in a binary choice, memories in the γ5β′2a and the γ4 failed to promote significant upwind movement (Figure 1I–J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1I-J.

claims.claim: Memories in the α1 and the β1β2 promoted steering and walking upwind in response to the CS+ odor.
claims.source: In contrast, memories in the α1 and the β1β2 promoted steering and walking upwind in response to the CS+ odor, compared to genetic controls and the 'No LED' control group of the same genotype (Figure 1I–J).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1I-J.

claims.claim: Memory in the α1 compartment reduced upwind locomotion in response to CS− odor compared to the genetic control groups.
claims.source: The memory in the α1 compartment also reduced upwind locomotion in response to CS− odor compared to the genetic control groups.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1I-J.

claims.claim: Memories in the α1 and β1β2 biased the direction of turning to steer toward upwind.
claims.source: By separately analyzing behaviors of individual flies based on their orientation at the onset of odors, we found that memories in the α1 and β1β2 biased the direction of turning to steer toward upwind (Figure 1K–L).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1K-L.

claims.claim: Memories in γ5β′2a and γ4 did not bias the turning direction.
claims.source: Memories in γ5β′2a and γ4 did not bias the turning direction, although they promoted flies initially facing downwind to change orientation in a non-directional manner (Figure 1K–L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and flies tended to orient toward upwind during CS+ odor presentation (Figure 1I).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1K-L and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: SS33917 and SS33918 driver lines showed the strongest upwind locomotion among the split-GAL4 drivers screened.
claims.source: Among the split-GAL4 drivers we screened, SS33917 and SS33918 showed the strongest upwind locomotion, especially at the onset of 10 s activation period (Videos 1 and 2; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: UpWiNs have extensive arborizations in the posterior dorsolateral area of the brain where MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 send converging axons.
claims.source: The UpWiNs have extensive arborizations in the posterior dorsolateral area of the brain where MBON-α1 (also known as MBON07) and MBON-α3 (also known as MBON14) send converging axons (Video 3; Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3A and Video 3.

claims.claim: DANs innervating the α1 and α3 compartments respond to sugar or electric shock/heat/bitter.
claims.source: DANs innervating the α1 and α3 compartments respond to sugar or electric shock/heat/bitter, and activation of DANs can substitute US to induce long-lasting appetitive and aversive memories, respectively (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Matheson et al., 2022; Pai et al., 2013; Schnitzer et al., 2022; Siju et al., 2020; Vrontou et al., 2021; Yamagata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Activation of DANs innervating the α1 and α3 compartments can substitute US to induce long-lasting appetitive and aversive memories, respectively.
claims.source: DANs innervating the α1 and α3 compartments respond to sugar or electric shock/heat/bitter, and activation of DANs can substitute US to induce long-lasting appetitive and aversive memories, respectively (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Matheson et al., 2022; Pai et al., 2013; Schnitzer et al., 2022; Siju et al., 2020; Vrontou et al., 2021; Yamagata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: MBON-α1 displays reduced odor response to an odor associated with activation of DANs in α1.
claims.source: MBON-α1 displays reduced odor response to an odor associated with activation of DANs in α1 (Yamada et al., 2023), whereas MBON-α3 increases response to an odor associated with sugar reward possibly due to interactions with appetitive memory compartments such as the β1 (Li et al., 2020; Plaçais et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2008) and decreases response to punishment-associated odors (Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Schnitzer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: MBON-α3 increases response to an odor associated with sugar reward possibly due to interactions with appetitive memory compartments such as the β1.
claims.source: MBON-α1 displays reduced odor response to an odor associated with activation of DANs in α1 (Yamada et al., 2023), whereas MBON-α3 increases response to an odor associated with sugar reward possibly due to interactions with appetitive memory compartments such as the β1 (Li et al., 2020; Plaçais et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2008) and decreases response to punishment-associated odors (Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Schnitzer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: MBON-α3 decreases response to punishment-associated odors.
claims.source: MBON-α1 displays reduced odor response to an odor associated with activation of DANs in α1 (Yamada et al., 2023), whereas MBON-α3 increases response to an odor associated with sugar reward possibly due to interactions with appetitive memory compartments such as the β1 (Li et al., 2020; Plaçais et al., 2013; Takemura et al., 2017; Tanaka et al., 2008) and decreases response to punishment-associated odors (Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Schnitzer et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Both MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 are required for retrieval of long-term appetitive memory.
claims.source: Both MBONs are required for retrieval of long-term appetitive memory (Ichinose et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Among 11 matched EM-reconstructed neurons of the UpWiNs, four neurons (one SMP353 and three SMP354 neurons) receive direct synaptic input from MBON-α1.
claims.source: Among 11 matched EM-reconstructed neurons of the UpWiNs, four neurons, one SMP353 and three SMP354 neurons, receive direct synaptic input from MBON-α1 (Figure 3B–E; Li et al., 2020; Scheffer et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3B-E.

claims.claim: SMP354 receives input from MBON-α3.
claims.source: SMP354 also receives input from MBON-α3; this strong convergent connectivity is exceptional among the population of the neurons that are postsynaptic to either of the MBONs (Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: The strong convergent connectivity of SMP354 receiving input from both MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 is exceptional among the population of neurons postsynaptic to either of the MBONs.
claims.source: SMP354 also receives input from MBON-α3; this strong convergent connectivity is exceptional among the population of the neurons that are postsynaptic to either of the MBONs (Figure 3D–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3D-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: UpWiNs that do not have direct connections with MBON-α1 or MBON-α3 receive indirect input from them via connections among UpWiNs.
claims.source: The rest of the UpWiNs do not have direct connections with these MBONs but receive indirect input from them via connections among UpWiNs (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: All the UpWiNs provide input to a single neuron, SMP108.
claims.source: Interestingly, all the UpWiNs provide input to a single neuron, SMP108 (Figure 3C), which has the highest number of connections with reward DANs and plays a key role in second-order conditioning (Yamada et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: SMP108 has the highest number of connections with reward DANs and plays a key role in second-order conditioning.
claims.source: Interestingly, all the UpWiNs provide input to a single neuron, SMP108 (Figure 3C), which has the highest number of connections with reward DANs and plays a key role in second-order conditioning (Yamada et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: The axon terminals of UpWiNs are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase.
claims.source: The axon terminals of UpWiNs are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase (Yamada et al., 2023), and therefore likely to be excitatory to the SMP108 and other downstream neurons.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation to support the claim.

claims.claim: UpWiNs are likely to be excitatory to the SMP108 and other downstream neurons.
claims.source: The axon terminals of UpWiNs are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase (Yamada et al., 2023), and therefore likely to be excitatory to the SMP108 and other downstream neurons.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the immunoreactivity to choline acetyltransferase.

claims.claim: A brief 10 ms stimulation of cholinergic MBON-α3 evoked a strong excitation in 3 out of 11 UpWiNs examined.
claims.source: A brief 10 ms stimulation of cholinergic MBON-α3 evoked a strong excitation in 3 out of 11 UpWiNs examined, whereas glutamatergic MBON-α1 evoked inhibitory responses in 4 out of 17 UpWiNs (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: Glutamatergic MBON-α1 evoked inhibitory responses in 4 out of 17 UpWiNs.
claims.source: A brief 10 ms stimulation of cholinergic MBON-α3 evoked a strong excitation in 3 out of 11 UpWiNs examined, whereas glutamatergic MBON-α1 evoked inhibitory responses in 4 out of 17 UpWiNs (Figure 4A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 4A-B.

claims.claim: The observed stochasticity of the connectivity between MBONs and UpWiNs is consistent with the EM connectome data.
claims.source: The observed stochasticity of the connectivity is consistent with the EM connectome data.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between functional and anatomical data.

claims.claim: MBON-α1 activation suppressed the excitatory effect of MBON-α3 when they were activated together.
claims.source: Moreover, MBON-α1 activation suppressed the excitatory effect of MBON-α3 when they were activated together (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 1 s photostimulation of a subset of UpWiNs evoked excitatory GCaMP response in both axons and dendrites of other UpWiNs.
claims.source: 1 s photostimulation evoked excitatory GCaMP response in both axons and dendrites (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: UpWiNs as a population receive and integrate synaptic inputs from MBONs that signal opposite signs of memory valence.
claims.source: These results indicate that as a population, UpWiNs receive and integrate synaptic inputs from MBONs that signal opposite signs of memory valence.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the functional connectivity experiments.

claims.claim: UpWiNs collectively receive olfactory information from the MBONs and lateral horn output neurons.
claims.source: The UpWiN cluster collectively receives olfactory information from the MBONs and lateral horn output neurons (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by anatomical data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Before training, UpWiNs showed relatively weak odor responses.
claims.source: Before training, the UpWiNs showed relatively weak odor responses (Figure 5B) likely because inhibitory and excitatory inputs cancel each other (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: After pairing an odor with optogenetic activation of reward DANs including those projecting to α1, UpWiNs displayed increased excitatory response to subsequent exposures to the CS+ odor but not to the CS− odor.
claims.source: After pairing an odor with optogenetic activation of reward DANs including those projecting to α1, UpWiNs displayed increased excitatory response to subsequent exposures to the CS+ odor but not to the CS− odor (Figure 5B–D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5B-D.

claims.claim: The enhancement of CS+ response in UpWiNs was observed irrespective of the identity of tested CS+ odors (OCT or MCH).
claims.source: We observed the enhancement of CS+ response irrespective of the identity of tested CS+ odors (OCT or MCH; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The enhancement of CS+ response in UpWiNs can be explained as an outcome of disinhibition from MBON-α1 whose output had been decreased by memory formation.
claims.source: This enhancement of CS+ response can be most easily explained as an outcome of disinhibition from MBON-α1 whose output had been decreased by memory formation; MBON-α1 is inhibitory to UpWiNs (Figure 4B) and MBON-α1 response to the CS+ is reduced following the same training protocol (Yamada et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data, with a citation to support the claim about MBON-α1 response reduction.

claims.claim: Plasticity in the β1 compartment may also contribute to the enhanced CS+ response in UpWiNs.
claims.source: In addition to such a mechanism, plasticity in the β1 compartment may also contribute to the enhanced CS+ response in UpWiNs because the driver R58E02-LexA contains DANs in the β1 and glutamatergic MBON from the β1 directly synapses on the dendrites of MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 (Takemura et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculation based on anatomical connectivity.

claims.claim: Only starved flies showed robust upwind locomotion upon UpWiN activation.
claims.source: First, the UpWiN activation phenotype was starvation dependent; only starved flies showed robust upwind locomotion upon UpWiN activation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Flies' response to UpWiN activation depended on the rate and direction of the airflow.
claims.source: Second, flies' response to UpWiN activation depended on the rate and direction of the airflow.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Flies did not move toward the periphery without airflow during UpWiN activation.
claims.source: Flies did not move toward the periphery without airflow (Video 4) and moved toward the center when the direction of airflow was reversed (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Video 4 and Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Flies moved toward the center when the direction of airflow was reversed during UpWiN activation.
claims.source: Flies did not move toward the periphery without airflow (Video 4) and moved toward the center when the direction of airflow was reversed (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Unilateral or bilateral ablation of aristae impaired movement toward the periphery during UpWiN activation.
claims.source: Finally, unilateral, or bilateral ablation of aristae, the wind-sensing organ in Drosophila (Yorozu et al., 2009), impaired movement toward the periphery during UpWiN activation (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: With unilateral ablation of arista, activation of UpWiNs still initiated turning but flies turned too much and failed to make a transition to forward walking toward upwind orientation.
claims.source: With unilateral ablation of arista, activation of UpWiNs still initiated turning but flies turned too much and failed to make a transition to forward walking toward upwind orientation (Video 5).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Video 5.

claims.claim: Flies transiently increased angular speed during the first ~300 ms of UpWiN activation.
claims.source: Flies transiently increased angular speed during the first ~300 ms (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The increased angular speed during the first ~300 ms of UpWiN activation was observed also in empty-split-GAL4 control flies and considered to be a startle response to activating light.
claims.source: This increased angular speed was observed also in empty-split-GAL4 control flies and considered to be a startle response to activating light.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: Direction of turning during the first ~300 ms of UpWiN activation was significantly biased toward the upwind direction when either of two lines for UpWiNs were used to express CsChrimson.
claims.source: However, direction of turning during this period was significantly biased toward the upwind direction when either of two lines for UpWiNs were used to express CsChrimson (Figure 6E–F).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6E-F.

claims.claim: UpWiNs activation modulated forward walking speed in a manner that depended on the orientation of flies at the onset of the activating light.
claims.source: UpWiNs activation also modulated forward walking speed in a manner that depended on the orientation of flies at the onset of the activating light (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: The orientation-dependent modulation of turning direction and walking speed observed during UpWiN activation is similar to that evoked by α1-specific memory.
claims.source: The orientation-dependent modulation of turning direction and walking speed observed is similar to that evoked by α1-specific memory (Figure 1K).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison between UpWiN activation and memory-driven behavior.

claims.claim: Activation of MBON-γ2α′1 with MB077B split-GAL4 modulated forward walking speed and promoted flies that already faced upwind to maintain that orientation but did not cause directional turning toward the upwind direction.
claims.source: In contrast, activation of MBON-γ2α′1 with MB077B split-GAL4 modulated forward walking speed and promoted flies that already faced upwind to maintain that orientation but did not cause directional turning toward the upwind direction (Figure 6D–G; see Figure 6—figure supplement 1 for other drivers).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 6D-G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: UpWiNs transform memory in an α1 into signals that promote olfactory navigation but do not yet specify lower-level motor parameters (i.e. turning direction and acceleration).
claims.source: These results are consistent with a view that UpWiNs transform memory in an α1 into signals that promote olfactory navigation but do not yet specify lower-level motor parameters (i.e. turning direction and acceleration).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the behavioral data.

claims.claim: Information about wind direction and UpWiN's activity needs to be integrated somewhere downstream to compute the turning direction.
claims.source: Information about wind direction and UpWiN's activity needs to be integrated somewhere downstream to compute the turning direction.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the behavioral data.

claims.claim: The central complex is the likely brain area for integration of wind direction and UpWiN's activity.
claims.source: The central complex is the likely brain area for such a computation (Matheson et al., 2022; Okubo et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Formation of long-lasting appetitive memory after odor-sugar conditioning relies on the DANs that innervate the α1 compartment.
claims.source: Formation of long-lasting appetitive memory after odor-sugar conditioning relies on the DANs that innervate the α1 compartment (Ichinose et al., 2021; Yamagata et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claims.claim: Control genotypes showed enhanced upwind locomotion in the presence of odors associated with sugar.

claims.claim: Flies that express the light chain of tetanus toxin (TNT) in UpWiNs showed compromised upwind locomotion in the presence of odors associated with sugar.
claims.source: The control genotypes showed enhanced upwind locomotion in the presence of odors associated with sugar, whereas flies that express the light chain of tetanus toxin (TNT) in UpWiNs showed compromised upwind locomotion (Figure 7A–B).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7A-B.

claims.claim: Blocking synaptic output of UpWiNs only during test period impaired preference to CS+ odor in binary choice compared to the genetic controls.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: UpWiNs play a major role in behavior during appetitive memory retrieval.
claims.source: These results indicate that UpWiNs play a major role in behavior during appetitive memory retrieval but also suggest that their behavioral contribution may not be limited to simple promotion of upwind locomotion.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genetic manipulation experiments.

claims.claim: Flies increased the probability of revisiting the location where UpWiNs activation was ended.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Optogenetic activation of the UpWiNs could bias spatial distribution of flies between quadrants with and without activating illumination.

claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The bias in spatial distribution caused by UpWiN activation is likely due to the airflow-independent function of UpWiNs.

claims.claim: UpWiN activation could increase the probability of revisiting behavior even in the absence of airflow.
claims.source: This bias is likely due to the airflow-independent function of UpWiNs because the UpWiN activation could increase the probability of revisiting behavior even in the absence of airflow (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by behavioral data in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The mode of synaptic integration observed in the UpWiNs matches the expectation from the valence-balance model.
claims.source: The mode of synaptic integration observed in the UpWiNs matches the expectation from this model.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claims.claim: When both presynaptic MBONs were activated, which mimicked the naive state, those inputs canceled each other, resulting in no net excitation.
claims.source: When both presynaptic MBONs were activated, which mimicked the naive state (i.e. no depression in either of the MBONs), those inputs canceled each other, resulting in no net excitation (Figure 4).

results.result: Appetitive memories stored in different mushroom body (MB) compartments induce different levels of upwind locomotion. Specifically, memories in α1 and β1β2 compartments promoted directional upwind steering and walking, while memories in γ5β'2a and γ4 compartments failed to promote significant upwind movement despite robust odor preference in binary choice assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19-C26, C117, and C136 collectively demonstrate compartment-specific behavioral strategies during memory retrieval, supported by extensive behavioral tracking data in Figure 1. The differential contributions to anemotaxis are well-documented through multiple behavioral parameters including turning direction, walking speed, and orientation-dependent responses.

results.result: UpWiNs (UpWind Neurons) were identified as a cluster of neurons postsynaptic to MBONs that can trigger robust upwind steering. These neurons have extensive arborizations where MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 converge, with four UpWiN neurons receiving direct synaptic input from MBON-α1, and SMP354 neurons showing exceptional convergent connectivity from both MBONs.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C27-C28, C35-C39, and C49 are well-supported by optogenetic screening data (Figure 2), anatomical EM connectome analysis (Figure 3), and multi-color flip-out imaging. The identification and characterization of UpWiNs as a convergence point for valence signals is robustly demonstrated through multiple complementary approaches.

results.result: UpWiNs integrate inhibitory and excitatory synaptic inputs from MBONs of appetitive (α1) and aversive (α3) memory compartments, respectively. Electrophysiological recordings showed that MBON-α3 evoked excitation in 3/11 UpWiNs while MBON-α1 evoked inhibition in 4/17 UpWiNs. When both MBONs were activated together, their inputs canceled each other, consistent with the valence-balance model.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C43-C48, and C79-C82 are strongly supported by whole-cell electrophysiology (Figure 4A-B) and two-photon calcium imaging (Figure 4C) demonstrating functional connectivity. The stochastic connectivity observed matches EM connectome predictions, and the cancellation of opposing inputs provides direct evidence for valence integration.

results.result: After appetitive memory formation, UpWiNs acquire enhanced responses to reward-predicting odors. Before training, UpWiNs showed weak odor responses, but after pairing odor with optogenetic activation of reward DANs, UpWiNs displayed increased excitatory responses to CS+ but not CS− odors. This enhancement is explained by disinhibition from MBON-α1 whose output decreases following memory formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C50-C54 are supported by electrophysiological recordings before and after training (Figure 5). The CS+-specific enhancement was observed regardless of odor identity (OCT or MCH), and the mechanistic explanation via MBON-α1 disinhibition is consistent with prior work showing depression of MBON-α1 responses after training.

results.result: Blocking UpWiNs impaired appetitive memory and reduced upwind locomotion during retrieval. Flies expressing tetanus toxin in UpWiNs showed compromised upwind locomotion compared to controls, and blocking synaptic output during test period impaired CS+ preference in binary choice.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C71-C74 are supported by genetic manipulation experiments using tetanus toxin (Figure 7A-B) and temperature-sensitive shibire (Figure 7C). The requirement of UpWiNs for both upwind locomotion and binary choice performance demonstrates their necessity for appetitive memory retrieval, though the authors note limitations in analyzing wind-directional behaviors with shibire experiments.

results.result: Photoactivation of UpWiNs increased the probability of flies returning to locations where activation was terminated, suggesting an additional role in olfactory navigation beyond simple upwind promotion. This revisiting behavior occurred even in the absence of airflow, indicating an airflow-independent function.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C75-C78 are supported by behavioral analysis of optogenetic activation experiments (Figure 2B, Figure 7D-E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The return probability phenotype is distinct from simple turning increases and persists without airflow, though the mechanistic basis for this spatial memory-like behavior requires further investigation.

results.result: UpWiN activation promotes wind-directed behaviors in a context-dependent manner. The upwind locomotion phenotype was starvation-dependent, required airflow, and depended on arista-mediated wind sensing. UpWiN activation biased turning direction toward upwind and modulated walking speed based on initial fly orientation, but did not specify lower-level motor parameters directly.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C68 are comprehensively supported by behavioral experiments manipulating starvation state (Figure 6A), airflow rate and direction (Figure 6B), arista ablation (Figure 6C), and detailed kinematic analysis (Figure 6D-G). The orientation-dependent modulation and comparison with MBON-γ2α'1 activation demonstrate that UpWiNs transform valence into navigational signals requiring downstream integration with wind direction information.

results.result: The convergent circuit motif observed in UpWiNs likely represents a general principle for valence integration in the MB downstream circuits. UpWiNs receive abundant input from lateral horn neurons, suggesting they integrate both innate and learned valences. Similar synaptic integration may control other components of olfactory behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are largely speculative predictions based on the current findings and anatomical connectivity data. While the convergent motif is well-established for UpWiNs (C83 supported by Li et al., 2020 citation), the broader generalization to other behaviors and the specific role in integrating innate/learned valences requires additional experimental validation beyond the anatomical evidence presented.

results.result: The central complex, particularly the fan-shaped body (FB), is the likely downstream integration site for UpWiN signals and wind direction information. UpWiNs project to FB neurons including FB6D, FB6I, and FB6T, which connect to hDelta neurons known to integrate wind-directional cues with odor information. SMP108, while prominent anatomically, showed different behavioral responses and was not required for memory retrieval.
results.evaluation: Claims C69, C105-C116 are supported by EM connectome analysis (Figure 3C), comparison with prior literature on FB function, and behavioral screening data (Figure 2). The identification of FB as the integration site is well-justified by anatomical connectivity and functional studies cited (Matheson et al., 2022), though direct functional validation of the UpWiN→FB pathway would strengthen these conclusions.

results.result: The use of divergent and convergent pathways to process valence signals represents an evolutionarily conserved strategy observed in both Drosophila MB circuits and vertebrate amygdala systems. In mammals, the amygdala is the primary site for valence assignment, with distinct networks diverging to different projection areas for aversive or appetitive responses, and convergent integration occurring in areas like the VTA.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C8-C13 establish the comparative context for the study through well-cited literature on mammalian valence processing. The parallel between fly and mammalian systems is appropriately supported by citations (Tye, 2018; Nieh et al., 2016; Beyeler et al., 2016; Namburi et al., 2015), providing strong conceptual framing for the significance of the UpWiN findings.

results.result: The Drosophila mushroom body serves as the primary site for CS-US association in olfactory learning, with parallel compartments defined by MBONs and DANs. Individual MBONs encode valence rather than odor identity or specific motor commands. MBON-α1 and MBON-α3 respond to sugar or punishment stimuli respectively, undergo learning-dependent plasticity, and are both required for long-term appetitive memory retrieval.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18, C29-C34 establish the well-characterized MB learning system through extensive citations to prior work (Aso et al., 2014a,b; Tanaka et al., 2008; Campbell et al., 2013; Hige et al., 2015b; Owald et al., 2015; Yamagata et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Plaçais et al., 2013; Jacob and Waddell, 2022; Schnitzer et al., 2022). This background is essential context and accurately represents the current understanding of the MB system.

results.result: UpWiN activation produces behavioral responses similar to moth pheromone navigation, with increased angular velocity and biased turning toward upwind on a similar ~200 ms timescale. This suggests UpWiNs may promote cast-surge-cast reactions during navigation of intermittent odor plumes.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C94 draw an interesting parallel between UpWiN function and moth navigation behavior (Cardé, 2021; Baker, 1990), supported by the temporal dynamics observed in Figure 6D-F. However, this remains speculative (C94) as the study did not directly test navigation in intermittent plumes or demonstrate the full cast-surge-cast sequence. The comparison is plausible but requires experimental validation.

results.result: UpWiNs have multiple functions beyond upwind surge: they can promote dopamine release in multiple MB compartments via SMP108 for second-order memory formation, may mediate upwind locomotion to innately attractive odors through lateral horn inputs, and could be the causal source of action correlates in DANs. All three functions likely contribute to olfactory navigation in complex environments.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C99 propose additional UpWiN functions based on anatomical connectivity and cited work (Yamada et al., 2023; Zolin et al., 2021). While C95 is supported by citation, C97-C98 are explicitly speculative and C99 is an inference. The role in innate odor responses and as a source of DAN action correlates requires direct experimental testing beyond the connectivity evidence presented.

results.result: Both flying and walking flies use wind-directed navigation strategies when encountering attractive odors. Airflow is detected by aristae and Johnston organ neurons, with left-right asymmetry computed in the central complex to represent wind direction. Fictive training with optogenetic DAN activation can promote or suppress upwind locomotion, indicating that memory retrieval utilizes the same navigational strategy as innate responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 synthesize prior work on Drosophila wind sensing and navigation (Álvarez-Salvado et al., 2018; Steck et al., 2012; van Breugel and Dickinson, 2014; Kamikouchi et al., 2006; Yorozu et al., 2009; Matheson et al., 2022; Okubo et al., 2020; Suver et al., 2019; Handler et al., 2019). These well-cited claims provide essential context for understanding how UpWiNs fit into the broader navigation circuitry.

results.result: Different MB compartments store distinct types of memories with different properties. The α1 compartment, which drives UpWiN-mediated upwind locomotion, forms memories slowly with weak DAN sugar responses but produces long-lasting, extinction-resistant memories. This suggests flies engage wind-guided navigation only when expecting robust/reliable rewards.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C123 are supported by extensive prior literature on compartment-specific memory properties (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Yamagata et al., 2015; Huetteroth et al., 2015; Ichinose et al., 2015; Yamada et al., 2023) and the current study's behavioral data (Figure 1E). The interpretation that α1 memory properties match expectations for reliable reward is logical, though the adaptive significance (C123) is somewhat speculative.

results.result: The MB circuit undergoes dramatic reorganization during metamorphosis, with adult-specific neurons (α/β KCs, MBON-α1, MBON-α3, MBON-β1>α) developing to support adult-specific anemotaxis behaviors. Larval-origin MBONs in γ and β' lobes persist but do not drive upwind locomotion. The adult-specific output pathways, including UpWiNs, may be dedicated to anemotaxis while larval-origin pathways support other behaviors like visual memory.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C135, C139-C143 are well-supported by developmental studies (Eichler et al., 2017; Truman et al., 2023; Pauls et al., 2010) and the current behavioral data showing differential compartment contributions (Figure 1). The hypothesis that adult-specific pathways are dedicated to anemotaxis (C142) is a reasonable inference from the anatomical and functional data, though direct developmental manipulation experiments would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: Appetitive memories in γ4 and γ5β'2a compartments can bias odor choice but do not promote upwind walking. This may be because the γ lobe stores both olfactory and visual memories, and walking upwind does not help approach visual cues associated with reward.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are supported by the behavioral data in Figure 1 showing compartment-specific differences, and the explanation is grounded in prior work showing γ lobe involvement in visual memory (Vogt et al., 2016; Vogt et al., 2014). The logic that upwind walking is inappropriate for visual cues is sound, though alternative explanations for the lack of upwind locomotion are not fully excluded.

results.result: SMP108 receives convergent input from all UpWiNs, has the highest number of connections with reward DANs, and plays a key role in second-order conditioning. UpWiN axon terminals are immunoreactive to choline acetyltransferase, indicating they are likely excitatory to SMP108 and other downstream neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42 are supported by EM connectome data (Figure 3C) and prior work (Yamada et al., 2023). The inference that cholinergic terminals are excitatory (C42) is standard and well-justified, though direct functional confirmation of the UpWiN→SMP108 connection would be valuable given that SMP108 blockade did not affect memory retrieval (C110).
